signals.summary: Epidermal pigmentation is a localized candidate morphology correlate, with anatomical-site/exposure sampling and psoriasis-specific biopsy selection as contextual alternatives.

candidates.title: Epidermal pigmentation
candidates.hypothesis: Variation in epidermal pigmentation may provide a localized visual correlate associated with the self-reported labels in this dataset.
features: Basal and suprabasal epidermal pigment amount and distribution
Pigment within lesion-free epidermis versus lesional tissue
limitations: Some supporting evidence uses electron microscopy beyond routine H&E resolution; visibility in routine sections requires testing.
Source populations and demographic definitions do not directly match the self-reported categories in this study.
Anatomical site and exposure may confound pigmentation comparisons. Pigmentation has not been established as a carrier of the model signal.

evidence.support: Electron microscopy of photoprotected volar forearm skin showed differing melanosome distribution patterns among the study-defined skin groups.
The studied human skin groups differed in epidermal melanin amount and composition.

candidates.title: Anatomical-site and exposure sampling
candidates.hypothesis: Differences in anatomical-site and exposure-related sampling could contribute through epidermal pigmentation, if their distributions differ across the dataset labels.
features: Epidermal pigment within matched anatomical sites
limitations: Protected and exposed samples differed in anatomical site as well as exposure.
Individual UV response is not captured reliably by demographic labels alone.
The distributions of site and exposure across this study's labels need to be checked.

evidence.support: Across the studied groups, chronically photoexposed skin had more epidermal melanin than corresponding photoprotected skin.
In an experimental UV study, measured erythemal sensitivity predicted DNA photodamage better than racial/ethnic origin or skin phototype.

candidates.title: Psoriasis-specific biopsy selection
candidates.hypothesis: Disease-specific biopsy selection could change the lesion mix across demographic labels within psoriasis samples.
features: Psoriasiform epidermal changes, spongiosis and inflammatory patterns within matched diagnoses
Prior treatment and refractory or atypical presentation
limitations: The supporting biopsy-frequency comparison comes from one health system and is specific to psoriasis.
Clinical histories and indications remain alternative explanations; these findings do not establish demographic differences in inflammatory morphology.
The selected biopsy histology series did not compare demographic groups.

evidence.support: Among adults with psoriasis in one academic health system, Black patients had higher adjusted odds of biopsy than White patients; the authors could not exclude differing clinical histories or presentations as explanations.
A clinically confirmed psoriasis biopsy series documented classic and non-classic histological features, illustrating variation among selected psoriasis biopsies.

limiting_evidence.support: Reported no significant epidermal or superficial dermal thickness difference and no observed collagen/elastic-fibre organization difference, alongside a dermal–epidermal junction difference. It does not justify a general dermal race signature.

signals.summary: Breast has the clearest directly measured H&E age-related precedent among these three examples: localized lobular changes and broader tissue composition. Neither has been shown to explain model predictions.

candidates.title: TDLU involution / epithelial cellularity
candidates.hypothesis: Age-associated TDLU involution and reduced epithelial cellularity could contribute to age-group prediction in breast tissue.
features: epithelial nuclear density in non-neoplastic lobules
limitations: Parity, menopause, diagnosis, and procedure may influence the sampled lobules.
Findings in normal or selected benign-biopsy cohorts may not transfer directly to this study's age groups and tissue mix.
The cited features have not been shown to carry the model prediction.

evidence.support: In normal breast samples from 1,938 women, TDLU count, span and acini count declined with age and were lower after menopause; parity also affected these measures.
Among 1,115 women with repeated benign breast biopsies, lobular involution generally progressed between biopsies, with variation by initial age and interval.

In H&E samples from donors aged 45 or younger, parity was associated with differences in TDLU/acini measures and recent childbirth with increased mononuclear cells; these features are not specific to chronological age.

candidates.title: Stromal–adipose tissue composition
candidates.hypothesis: Age-associated differences in stromal and adipose area fractions, together with epithelial cellularity, could provide a broader tissue-composition cue.
limitations: Cross-sectional tissue fractions do not demonstrate longitudinal adipose replacement.
Epithelial area did not show a universal linear decline with age; reported composition changes plateaued around age 55.
BMI, parity, menopause, procedure, tumor proximity, and tissue processing may influence observed morphology.
Measured composition is not evidence that the prediction model uses these features.

evidence.support: In histologically normal H&E breast tissue from 454 surgical patients, epithelial nuclear density declined with age; stromal area decreased and adipose area increased until roughly age 55, then plateaued. Epithelial area lacked a significant age trend, as did stromal and adipose nuclear density.
evidence.locator: 3. Results, 3.2. Associations between age and tissue morphometry

limiting_evidence.support: In a Nurses’ Health Studies benign-biopsy cohort, quantitative and qualitative involution measures did not predict subsequent breast cancer after the reported adjustments; this limits risk interpretation, not the existence of age-related histology.
limiting_evidence.locator: Results: TDLU involution measures and breast cancer risk; Discussion

signals.summary: In the targeted literature search, no sufficiently supported direct morphology explanation for the full gastric residual signal was identified.

candidates.title: Gastric cancer subtype composition
candidates.hypothesis: Within gastric cancer samples, sex-associated differences in subtype composition could provide a disease-dependent cue if incompletely represented by the diagnosis matching.
limitations: Within-cancer subtype proportions are not population incidence; age and referral selection affect these comparisons.
Signet-ring and diffuse histology are not interchangeable categories.
Studies reporting similar diffuse-type rates limit generalization. The cancer-only findings do not explain the full tissue cohort.

evidence.support: In a Beijing hospital series of 2,199 gastric cancer patients, signet-ring histology comprised a larger fraction of cancers in women than men. This was a within-cancer subtype proportion, not female predominance in population incidence; Lauren classification was available for only 255 patients.
evidence.locator: Methods: Patients and data collection; Results: Patient characteristics

evidence.support: In 2,983 surgically treated gastric adenocarcinoma patients in Korea, diffuse histology was more frequent among women, especially younger women; diffuse histology was also more common at younger ages in both sexes.

A Norwegian series found similar sex-specific rates of diffuse gastric cancer but higher intestinal-type rates in men. Subtype proportions among cancer patients and population incidence rates are different quantities.

candidates.title: Infection, site, and treatment-dependent mucosal context
candidates.hypothesis: Within relevant benign gastric disease samples, H. pylori history and site-dependent metaplasia/inflammation could be conditional context cues associated with sex.
features: atrophy as a checked covariate, not a presumed universal sex feature
limitations: Infection, anatomical site, age, and eradication history affect mucosal findings.
A metaplasia difference coexisted with no significant sex difference in atrophy after eradication.
Molecular interleukin-8 results are a distinct endpoint, not a visible H&E feature.
These disease-dependent observations do not establish broad gastric sexual dimorphism or a hormonal explanation.

evidence.support: In 172 patients followed after H. pylori eradication, intestinal metaplasia scores were higher in men before eradication and at most follow-up points, whereas atrophy scores did not differ significantly by sex.

In selected patients with benign gastric disease, H. pylori-associated antral inflammatory activity and corpus atrophy/metaplasia varied with sex, age and site; the abstract reports no sex difference in interleukin-8 mRNA induction.

limiting_evidence.support: A Scottish study including gastric and oesophageal adenocarcinomas found male predominance for intestinal subtype but similar diffuse-type incidence between sexes; pooled upper-GI evidence is indirect for gastric tissue alone.
limiting_evidence.locator: Abstract: METHOD AND MATERIALS and RESULTS
